title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
The core failure here is a training-data sourcing problem. Udio built and deployed an AI music generation system using copyrighted recordings without obtaining licenses from rights holders first. The infringement, if proven, happened at the model-building stage, before any user ever typed a prompt, meaning the problem was embedded in the system long before it reached the public.

Several major labels sued Udio over this practice, alleging that well-known recordings were used without permission or payment. Universal Music Group and Warner Music Group each reached settlements and moved toward licensing agreements with Udio. Sony Music filed additional lawsuits, including one asserting claims over more than 30,000 recordings. A class action brought by independent artists was allowed to proceed after a court declined to dismiss it. A musicians' union also filed a separate lawsuit challenging UMG's settlement arrangement with Udio.

None of the lawsuits have produced final verdicts on whether Udio's training constituted copyright infringement, and the financial terms of the settlements are not public. The allegations are claims made in litigation, not established findings of fact.

summary:
Universal Music Group has reached a settlement with AI music startup Udio, ending a lawsuit that accused the company of using copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence system. Under the agreement, Udio will launch a new platform next year that uses only authorized and licensed music. Users will be able to create original songs through text prompts, and participating artists will receive compensation, though specific financial terms were not disclosed. UMG's leadership stated the settlement reflects their commitment to supporting artists while embracing new technologies.

The dispute originated from allegations that Udio had used famous songs like The Temptations' "My Girl" to train its AI model, which then generated similar melodies without permission or payment. Udio, founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees and backed by investors including will.i.am and Andreessen Horowitz, had defended its technology as a learning process similar to how musicians study existing work. This licensing agreement marks Udio's first major deal with a major music label and signals a potential shift toward industry cooperation on AI music creation.
